item.title: ICBM DF-61 enters routine training with PLA Rocket Force; rapid transition highlights faster-than-usual development: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 22:32:00
DF-61 Photo: VCG China's new DF-61 intercontinental ballistic missile, which first debuted at the September 2025 military parade, has been inducted into the People's Liberation Army Rocket Force and is now a part of routine training, according to a report by state broadcaster China Central Television (CCTV) on Thursday. A military expert said the pace at which the DF-61 moved from its public debut to routine training was much faster than the traditional combat-capability development cycle for intercontinental ballistic missiles. The disclosure came as China marked the 66th anniversary of the successful launch of its first domestically manufactured short-range surface-to-surface missile, the DF-1. The rapid transition indicates that the missile had already completed required procedures before its public unveiling, according to military commentator Shao Yongling. "Firstly, this shows that it had already completed development, finalization, trial deployment and reliability verification before its appearance, indicating a high level of technological maturity," Shao was quoted as saying in the CCTV report. The military commentator attributed the progress to the Rocket Force's established equipment support and training systems. The DF-61 is compatible with existing command, communications and logistical support networks, while the Rocket Force's accumulated experience in organizing and conducting training for intercontinental ballistic missiles has enabled units to become familiar with the new equipment more quickly after receiving it, Shao noted. This has helped shorten the process of generating combat capabilities and reflects the progress made in the Rocket Force's development under the strategic requirement of being capable of both nuclear and conventional operations and conducting deterrence across all domains, she added. According to Shao, the DF-61's participation in routine training means it has become part of practical training exercises involving field mobility, position changes and launch procedures. Its induction into service represents an upgrade to China's land-based nuclear counterstrike capabilities, strengthening the force's mobile survivability and penetration capabilities, she said. The DF-61 made its first public appearance during the military parade in Beijing on September 3, 2025, marking the 80th anniversary of the victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War. It was displayed in the strategic strike formation alongside other advanced strategic missile systems, including the air-launched Jinglei-1, or JL-1, the submarine-launched Julang-3, or JL-3, and the DF-31BJ land-based intercontinental ballistic missile. The latest disclosure comes 66 years after China's first domestically manufactured short-range surface-to-surface missile, the DF-1, was successfully launched. On November 5, 1960, China's first domestically manufactured short-range surface-to-surface missile, designated 1059 and later named the DF-1, was successfully launched at the Jiuquan missile test site. Although the DF-1 was a reverse-engineered version of the Soviet Union-made short-range R-2 missile and was never deployed as an operational weapon, its successful test marked a foundational step in China's missile development, Shao noted. Shao added that the DF-1 occupies a pioneering position in the country's missile and defense science and technology history, as it laid the groundwork for subsequent advances. More importantly, the program enabled China to accumulate essential expertise, infrastructure and institutional experience, which directly supported the subsequent "Eight Years, Four Missiles" development plan, she said. The experience laid the groundwork for the independent development of the DF-2, the integration of nuclear warheads with missiles, and subsequent efforts to develop intercontinental and submarine-launched missiles, Shao added. From the first successful launch of the 1059 missile in the Gobi Desert to the induction of the DF-61 into the Rocket Force, China's strategic missile development has undergone more than six decades of evolution, the expert noted.

item.title: One year on, Fujian carrier pushes toward full combat capability
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 21:12:00
The commissioning and flag-presenting ceremony of the Fujian, China's first aircraft carrier equipped with electromagnetic catapults, is held at a naval port in Sanya City, South China's Hainan Province, on November 5, 2025. Photo: Xinhua November 5 marks the first anniversary of the commissioning of China's third aircraft carrier Fujian . Officially inducted on November 5, 2025, the Fujian is the first catapult-equipped carrier fully designed and built by China, and the world's first conventionally powered carrier with electromagnetic catapults. In its first year, the Fujian sailed south through the Taiwan Straits to the South China Sea, then north to the East China Sea and Yellow Sea, completing cross-theater trials and training, showing it can operate across sea zones in the far seas, with coordination with escorting vessels reaching a certain level, CCTV News reported on Thursday. CCTV reported that 2026 has been a critical year for the Fujian 's transition from initial combat capability to full combat capability. Military affairs experts told the Global Times that the Fujian has completed its leap from platform validation to system integration in its first year, and is pushing toward "full combat capability" through high-intensity training, propelling the PLA Navy into an era of three-carrier rotation. Initial combat capability Before the Fujian entered service, its activities were already being closely watched. On June 17, 2022, China's third aircraft carrier was launched and named the Fujian , with hull number 18. On May 1, 2024, the Fujian completed its first eight-day sea trial, testing propulsion, electrical and other systems, meeting expected targets. On September 22, 2025, the J-15T heavy fighter jet, the J-35 stealth fighter jet, and the KJ-600 early warning aircraft - all displayed at the 2025 V-Day parade - completed their first catapult takeoffs and landings aboard the Fujian , reported CCTV. After being officially commissioned, within half a month, it formed a carrier group with multiple vessels for its first live maritime training, with multiple carrier-based aircraft completing numerous catapult takeoffs and landings, validating the Fujian's electromagnetic catapult, recovery and deck operations, CCTV reported. Zhang Junshe, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Thursday that the Fujian now has cross-theater far-sea operational capability, with coordination with escorting vessels reaching a certain level, meaning it has basically formed combat capability. "Basically formed combat capability" means the Fujian can sail normally; its aircraft can take off and land on deck, and it can conduct basic formation training with escort vessels. "Full combat capability" requires a leap from "can sail, can take off and land, can fight limited battles" to "can conduct high-intensity, all-weather, system-based, sustained operations." At the same time, all ships in the group must coordinate closely to ensure the carrier strike group can sustain system-based operations in the far seas, Zhang said. The Fujian is now tackling these requirements one by one through high-intensity training. Zhang said three points of interest should be observed: first, full-deck, full-load sortie generation, upgrading from "can use catapult" to "can use catapult continuously at high intensity"; second, takeoffs and landings under complex conditions. Nighttime and severe sea states are recognized difficulties, and pilots must obtain night qualifications; third, deep integration of the formation system, achieving integrated command and information sharing between ships and aircraft. Far-sea training Far-sea training is the final piece of the puzzle for full combat capability, Song Zhongping, another Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Thursday. Since October 14, the PLA Navy's Liaoning carrier group has been training in relevant waters of the Western Pacific, a routine mission under the annual plan, aimed at testing and improving combat-oriented training and continuously enhancing mission capability. It complies with international law and practice and does not target any specific country or target, according to China's Ministry of Defense. Against this backdrop, Song said that given the past year's progress, the Fujian may soon be able to conduct similar far-sea training. Song explained that the Fujian has grown in three ways over its first year. First, after prolonged trial service, its hull lines, internal structure, electrical and propulsion systems and electromagnetic catapult support systems have all been effectively tested. "This is China's first large carrier with a flat deck. The Fujian 's first year shows its design is sound and meets China's actual needs for developing large carriers." Second, ship-aircraft coordination has produced substantive results. The Fujian has initial aviation combat, support and sustained operation capabilities. Third, it has begun building out the carrier strike group system. Over the past year, the Fujian has conducted multiple compatibility drills with escort vessels, practicing formation navigation, command coordination and joint ship-aircraft support. "This step is laying the foundation for a complete carrier strike group," Song said. Within a year, the Fujian jumped from "multiple carrier aircraft catapult takeoffs and landings, initial full-deck capability" to "live formation training, cross-theater maneuvers", with escort coordination reaching a certain level and initial combat capability achieved. "This pace is rare in the history of global carrier development, completing in one year what other countries took years to do." Song said the next step may see the Fujian carrier strike group head into the Western Pacific, or even more unfamiliar and complex waters, for far-sea deployments and combat-oriented trials, testing sustained operations, logistics support and adaptability to complex sea conditions. Value of three carriers With the Liaoning , Shandong and Fujian , the PLA Navy has entered the three-carrier era. "The real value of the three-carrier era is not the visual impact of three ships in one frame, but the system of rotation among 'on duty - training - maintenance'," Zhang stressed. Three carriers form the minimum threshold for sustained maritime presence: one on duty, one in training, and one in maintenance. Once rotation runs smoothly, carriers upgrade from scarce resources "pulled out when needed" to strategic tools "ready at any time." It's also possible the Fujian will conduct dual- or even triple-carrier group exercises with the Liaoning and Shandong , Song said. Such drills would be significant: they would show that China can mobilize multiple large carriers simultaneously, and dual- or triple-carrier drills with other services would be more targeted and closer to real combat. This means the Fujian strike group's deployment will gradually shift from "validating performance" to "fulfilling missions", and from "training the platform" to "training for the mission", Song said.

item.title: Chinese counter-drone laser downs waves of drones in Gobi Desert test, overcomes key technical hurdles
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04 22:20:00
Photo: Science and Technology Daily In a desert in Northwest China, waves of suicide drones flying at low altitude from multiple directions suddenly burst into flames, lose control and crash before reaching their target. This scene isn't from a sci-fi film, but from a recent field test of the "Guangjian" series of laser powered counter-drone systems developed by the AVIC Manufacturing Technology Institute. "Over the years, we have focused on key technologies that constrain the performance of counter-drone laser systems and made sustained efforts to overcome them, tackling challenges in optical fiber drawing, heat dissipation and temperature control, and precision targeting," Zhou Shuiliang, a lab director at the institute, was quoted as saying in a report released by the Science and Technology Daily on Wednesday. The progress highlights the potential of laser weapons as a means of countering the growing threat posed by drones. "Laser weapons are a type of directed-energy weapon that can engage low, slow, and small aerial targets, such as drones, at relatively low cost. They can serve as a supplement to short-range air and missile defense systems," military affairs expert Song Zhongping told the Global Times on Wednesday. "Unlike conventional interception methods such as missiles, laser beams travel at nearly 300,000 kilometers per second. At typical air defense engagement distances, the time they take to reach a target is virtually negligible, giving laser weapons the advantage in rapid response," Song said. However, shooting down a drone with a laser weapon is not simply a matter of pointing a beam at it. Song explained that the system relies on a complete early-warning and fire-control system to detect, track and lock onto a target before concentrating laser fire on it. "Although a laser beam travels extremely fast, it must remain focused on a target long enough to inflict sufficient damage on its exterior, internal circuitry or critical components to destroy it," he said. "The types of targets that can be engaged, as well as the damage inflicted, vary with the weapon's power." This helps explain why the challenges facing the Guangjian development team went beyond simply making the laser more powerful. According to Zhou, laser energy must be transmitted and amplified through specialty optical fibers. These fibers are doped with special rare-earth elements and have a structure different from that of conventional optical fibers, making consistent manufacturing particularly demanding. Previously, technicians had to rely on experience to manually adjust multiple parameters during the fiber-drawing process, with even slight fluctuations potentially affecting fiber quality. The team subsequently introduced an intelligent, multivariable control system that uses algorithms to coordinate adjustments to production parameters, improving both drawing efficiency and product yield, according to the Science and Technology Daily. Improving the fibers brought another challenge into focus: heat. As laser systems become more powerful and compact, heat can build up rapidly in a limited space. Without effective cooling, the equipment may struggle to operate reliably for extended periods. Bai Zhen, a member of the research team, told the Daily that the team had developed a phase-change cooling material that used paraffin as its base. In simple terms, the material absorbs a large amount of heat as it melts, acting like a compact heat absorber for the laser system, Bai explained. After adjusting the material formula and packaging design, the team carried out a test during which the laser operated continuously for 30 minutes while maintaining stable temperatures. Improvements in heat management are important for ensuring that lasers can operate reliably over extended periods, a key factor in their practical use against drones. In Song's view, the main advantages of laser weapons are their rapid response and relatively low cost per interception, making them particularly suitable for dealing with low-cost aerial threats such as drones. During the test, multiple waves of suicide drones approached a target at low altitude from different directions, simulating a complex aerial threat. As they closed in, they were hit by lasers, causing them to catch fire and then crash before reaching their target, thereby demonstrating the system's ability to intercept incoming threats under challenging conditions.

item.title: Japan claims it spotted Chinese WZ-7 drone passing through Miyako Strait; Chinese expert says flights normal
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03 22:20:00
A Chinese WZ-7 high-altitude reconnaissance drone Photo: VCG Japan's Defense Ministry Joint Staff claimed on Monday that Chinese WZ-7 high-altitude reconnaissance drone had flown through the Miyako Strait, which connects the East China Sea and the Pacific Ocean, twice on the same day. The claim comes as China's Liaoning aircraft carrier group continues carrying out far seas training as announced by the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) Navy. The Miyako Strait is an important passage that vessels and aircraft from various countries use to enter and exit the Western Pacific, and the Chinese drone's flights through the waterway were entirely normal, Zhang Junshe, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Tuesday. As such, Japan should not make a fuss about such activities, Zhang said. The WZ-7, also known as the Xianglong, or Soaring Dragon, is an independently developed Chinese high-altitude, long-endurance strategic reconnaissance drone. It measures 14 meters in length and has a wingspan of 22.8 meters. Featuring a distinctive joined-wing aerodynamic configuration, the aircraft can carry synthetic aperture radar, high-resolution digital cameras, infrared thermal imaging equipment and electronic reconnaissance systems, according to China National Radio. With an operational ceiling of around 20,000 meters, the drone is designed for all-weather, round-the-clock reconnaissance. According to Zhang, the WZ-7 has an endurance of approximately 10 to 12 hours and a cruising speed of around 800 kilometers per hour. These capabilities allow it to remain in the air for extended periods over the Miyako Strait, the East China Sea and the Western Pacific, potentially maintaining continuous surveillance of maritime targets, he said. "The two flights on the same day may have been intended to ensure uninterrupted maritime surveillance," Zhang noted, adding that "such operations are consistent with the drone's normal operational characteristics." The WZ-7's reconnaissance capabilities can be summarized as seeing farther and longer while operating in different weather and lighting conditions, Zhang said. Its optical and infrared sensors, together with synthetic aperture radar, enable it to collect high-resolution images during the day, detect heat sources at night and conduct radar imaging even in cloudy, rainy or low-light conditions. The aircraft can also conduct wide-area searches, pinpoint targets and identify them at high resolution, providing maritime formations with information on the surrounding operational environment, Zhang said. He stressed that the WZ-7 is a reconnaissance and surveillance platform, rather than an attack aircraft. The Japanese release claimed that the Japan Air Self-Defense Force scrambled fighter jets in response. The ministry also released photos of the WZ-7's flights. Zhang noted that photographs released by Japan showed the WZ-7's belly, suggesting that the WZ-7 was flying at a higher altitude than the Japanese fighters. The Japanese Air Self-Defense Force possibly deployed the F-15 fighter, according to Zhang. When carrying weapons and external fuel tanks, such fighters generally cruise at altitudes of around 12,000 to 14,000 meters, below the WZ-7's operating altitude of approximately 20,000 meters, he said. On October 25, a CCTV News report commented on Japan's footage of another Chinese WZ-7 high-altitude reconnaissance drone, also shot from below that time, indicating a significant altitude gap between the filming aircraft and the WZ-7. "The drone's maximum flight altitude is about 19,000 to 20,000 meters. If Japan can only look up to observe, locate and track the aircraft, it means Japanese assets cannot reach that altitude. At its maximum height, the drone's reconnaissance abilities, early warning signal transmission and connectivity can reach a new level. This shows that China's air and sea advantages are being rapidly established in the relevant waters," military commentator Du Wenlong was quoted as saying. "Overall, the WZ-7's flights over the waters of the East China Sea and the Western Pacific were normal activities in airspace over international waters or areas open to international navigation and flight, and were consistent with international law and practice," Zhang said. US and Japanese high-altitude reconnaissance aircraft have also conducted surveillance flights over the East China Sea and the Western Pacific for years, he noted. Japan should therefore view China's reconnaissance flights with a normal mindset, rather than apply double standards or use the incident to sensationalize the so-called "China threat" rhetoric, Zhang added. Japan has frequently claimed it spotted PLA vessel and aircraft activities since the PLA Navy's Liaoning carrier group began training in the Western Pacific. The PLA Navy announced on October 14 that it had dispatched the Liaoning carrier group to conduct training in the Western Pacific. The PLA Navy said the deployment was a routine training mission carried out as part of the country's annual plan and is aimed at testing and improving combat-oriented training and continuously enhancing the ability to fulfill missions. It complies with relevant international laws and practice and does not target any specific country or target.

item.title: China-Russia military ties advance with significant progress in high-level exchanges and joint military exercises: China's CMC vice chairman
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03 19:01:00
China Russia Photo: Xinhua Zhang Shengmin, vice chairman of the Central Military Commission (CMC) met with visiting Russian Defense Minister Andrei Belousov at the Diaoyutai State Guesthouse in Beijing on Tuesday, China’s Ministry of National Defense (MND) announced on Tuesday. Zhang said that this year marks the 30th anniversary of the establishment of the China-Russia strategic partnership of coordination and the 25th anniversary of the signing of the China-Russia Treaty of Good-Neighborliness and Friendly Cooperation. Under the strategic guidance of the two heads of state, China-Russia relations have entered a new stage of more substantive engagement and faster development, playing a constructive role in maintaining global strategic stability and improving global governance. Zhang said that China-Russia military ties have in recent years advanced alongside broader bilateral relations, with significant progress in high-level exchanges and joint military exercises and training. China stands ready to work with Russia to fully implement the important consensus reached by the two heads of state, keep strengthening strategic communication, enhance mutual trust in the military field, improve cooperation mechanisms, and explore new areas of cooperation that reflect the characteristics of the times, in a bid to safeguard their respective sovereignty, security and development interests and uphold global and regional stability. Belousov said that, under the strategic guidance of the two heads of state, China-Russia strategic partnership of coordination in the new era has continued to deepen and reached an unprecedentedly high level, which is of vital importance to peace, stability and prosperity in both countries and the world, according to the MND. At present, the international security situation, particularly in the Asia-Pacific region, is complex and volatile. Russia appreciates and supports China’s active role in major international and regional affairs. Russia is willing to continue close coordination with China, strengthen strategic consultations, firmly support each other, expand practical cooperation in areas such as military education and scientific and technological innovation, and achieve further progress in relations between the two countries and their armed forces, Belousov said. Chinese and Russian naval vessels sail in formation towards the designated sea area during the maritime phase of the "Joint Sea-2026" exercise between China and Russia, July 10, 2026. Photo: Xinhua The “Joint Sea-2026” exercise between China and Russia concluded at a military port in Qingdao in East China’s Shandong Province on July 13. Launched on July 6 the joint exercise is the 12th in the series dating back to 2012. The joint naval exercises have become a key platform for China-Russia naval cooperation, strengthening their capabilities for combined maritime operations. Song Zhongping, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Tuesday that China and Russia maintain extensive military cooperation, spanning joint exercises and training, naval and air force exchanges, and counterterrorism efforts under the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) framework, reflecting the high level of ties between their armed forces. The new areas of China-Russia cooperation that reflect the characteristics of the times include opposing hegemony and power politics, as well as upholding a multipolar world order, Song said. Song added that China and Russia share broad common ground in opposing hegemony and power politics and upholding the post-World War II international order, making their cooperation important for regional and global peace.

item.title: China's HQ-9B air defense missile intercepts new maneuvering missiles in test
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-02 23:16:00
Photo: CCTV During a new weapons verification mission, a Chinese ground-based air defense unit demonstrated its ability to intercept new-type missile targets, including ballistic missiles and one missile that suddenly changed direction during flight, according to a report by state broadcaster China Central Television (CCTV) on Monday. The operation, involving China's HQ-9B surface-to-air missile system, saw the Central Theater Command Air Force's "Shenwei Missile Battalion" successfully intercept two new types of missile targets. "On the day of the mission, we hadn't yet been assigned which targets we would engage. We knew there were several types of targets, including ballistic missiles, but we didn't know that our unit would be the one tasked with intercepting them," Shi Shidong, a member of the battalion, was quoted by CCTV as saying in the report. When one of the incoming missiles suddenly changed direction and rapidly descended, personnel from the Central Theater Command Air Force's ground-to-air missile force, involving the HQ-9B surface-to-air missile system, reacted within seconds and launched an interceptor before the engagement window closed, CCTV reported. "It suddenly descended sharply. If you fail to act for two seconds, or even one second, and do not launch in advance, you could miss the window," Shi said. The unit's quick decision-making ensured the emergency launch successfully intercepted the target. The report also highlighted the importance of an integrated command and information-sharing system in shortening response times. Military commentator Song Zhongping told the Global Times that intercepting a maneuvering ballistic missile places additional demands on the HQ-9B's guidance and maneuvering capabilities. The system uses a combination of active radar and inertial guidance, he said. "Intercepting a maneuvering ballistic missile becomes more difficult. On the one hand, the active radar seeker must accurately track and lock onto the warhead of the incoming ballistic missile. At the same time, the interceptor itself must maneuver rapidly to keep up with changes in the target's trajectory," Song told the Global Times, before noting that the interceptor must maintain a lock and respond quickly when the target changes course, or it could miss the opportunity to engage. "This places high demands on the HQ-9B's maneuverability and its actuation system. It needs to react as quickly as possible, including through thrust-vector control, to track a ballistic missile that has changed its trajectory and effectively intercept it," he said. Hu Yang, another member of the battalion, told CCTV that the interval between receiving a target warning from higher-level command and completing an interception could be as short as two minutes. Song said this reflected the development of an integrated network for information sharing and command, which enables rapid early warnings, target tracking and allocation. "The system allows different air defense missile units to be connected. Targets can be assigned to the most suitable interceptor, with priority given to the nearest available unit, so that an engagement can be carried out in the most effective way," he said. According to CCTV, the unit has intercepted various types of targets and destroyed multiple types of missiles during training and exercises in recent years. In another engagement involving maritime targets, it simultaneously countered multiple incoming missiles approaching at both high and low altitudes. Military expert Zhang Xuefeng told CCTV that China's ground-based air defense missile systems had reached the forefront of the world's top-tier systems. At the 2025 military parade marking the 80th anniversary of the victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression, China displayed a range of advanced air and missile defense systems, including the HQ-9B, HQ-9C, HQ-19 and HQ-29. These systems can contribute to a layered, multi-stage air and missile defense network, with integrated information support further improving interception efficiency, Zhang noted. Song echoed the viewpoint, saying improvements in information technology and intelligent systems, as well as the integration of different weapons systems and the coordination of their coverage ranges made it practical. The successful intercept test also raised the possibility that the HQ-9B can intercept hypersonic missiles. Song said this depends on the flight trajectory of the particular weapon. "Hypersonic missiles do travel at very high speeds. When using systems such as the HQ-9B and HQ-9C to intercept them, the approach would rely more on head-on interception. This places high demand on detecting and locking onto hypersonic targets and tracking their changing trajectories," Song said. "As the PLA air and missile defense system continues to improve, intercepting hypersonic weapons in the true sense is also possible," he said.

item.title: China, Vietnam to hold second joint counter-terrorism exercise in Hanoi
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-02 20:44:00
The China-Vietnam joint counter-terrorism training is underway, in Nanning, South China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region on July 27, 2024. File photo: Xinhua The Chinese People's Armed Police Force and the mobile police force under the Vietnamese Ministry of Public Security are set to conduct a joint counter-terrorism exercise, codded "Cooperation-2026," in Hanoi, Vietnam, in early to mid-November, China's Ministry of National Defense announced on Monday. The exercise, themed around joint efforts to "combat violent terrorist crimes," will cover a range of training subjects, including explosive ordnance detection and disposal, ground maneuvering and assaults on high-rise buildings, according to the announcement. This will be the second exercise of its kind between the two countries and is expected to deepen exchanges and cooperation in counter-terrorism while enhancing their capabilities for joint operations, the ministry said. The inaugural exercise, held in 2024 in Southwest China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, was aimed at addressing shared concerns over terrorist threats and focused on joint efforts to combat violent terrorist activities, according to the Xinhua News Agency. During the two-week exercise, Chinese and Vietnamese personnel conducted training across seven categories and 27 subjects, including exchanges and discussions, command, skills, water-based operations, tactical coordination, specialized counterterrorism drills and comprehensive counterterrorism exercises. The program also featured sports competitions and cultural performances. Compared with the inaugural exercise, this year's training will take place in Vietnam and focus on several key urban counter-terrorism operations, Wang Yunfei, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Monday. The first exercise covered a relatively broad range of subjects, including water-based training and comprehensive tactical drills across different scenarios. The upcoming exercise places greater emphasis on explosive ordnance disposal, ground maneuvering and building-entry operations, which are particularly relevant to counter-terrorism missions in complex urban environments, Wang said. The change of venue is also significant, as conducting the exercise in Hanoi will allow personnel from both sides to become more familiar with the operational environment in Vietnam and practice coordination under conditions closer to those they may encounter during actual counter-terrorism missions there, he noted. "The move also demonstrates growing mutual trust between the two sides," Wang said, adding that "training will also help improve coordination in command procedures, tactical cooperation and joint responses to security threats." "The two countries could also explore further cooperation in the application of unmanned equipment," Wang said. The program in 2024 featured a number of unmanned systems, including robotic dogs, biomimetic robotic birds and wall-climbing robots, which were used in coordinated operations. Virtual reality (VR) and mixed reality (MR) technologies were also employed to create simulated confrontation scenarios, according to the China Youth Daily. Such technologies have increasingly become important tools in counter-terrorism training, allowing personnel to practice responding to complex scenarios while improving coordination between human operators and unmanned platforms, said Wang, adding that the upcoming exercise could feature further technological upgrades, although its specific equipment and arrangements have yet to be announced. In his view, the selection of training subjects for the 2026 exercise also reflects the challenges posed by terrorist activities in densely populated urban areas, where high-rise buildings, complicated structures and potential explosive threats can make operations particularly difficult. Explosive ordnance disposal, rapid ground maneuvering and assaults on high-rise buildings address several key challenges in such scenarios, requiring participating personnel to improve their ability to respond quickly, coordinate movements and carry out precise operations in complex environments, he noted. Beyond the military and operational aspects, the exercise also carries broader significance for bilateral security cooperation. Against a backdrop of complex and evolving regional security challenges, closer counter-terrorism coordination between China and Vietnam will help the two countries strengthen their ability to address cross-border terrorist threats and transnational crimes, while contributing to security and stability in the region, Wang said. Looking ahead, the two sides could explore expanding cooperation into areas such as intelligence sharing, cross-border law enforcement operations, joint training involving unmanned equipment and emergency rescue, he added.

item.title: China's state media gives key details on China's upgraded J-20A, J-20S stealth fighters
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-01 21:25:00
A model of a J-20 stealth fighter on display at the 2026 Nanchang Aviation Industry Expo held in Nanchang, East China's Jiangxi Province, on October 31, 2026 Photo: VCG Chinese state media on Sunday revealed new details about the evolution of China's J-20 stealth fighter family, highlighting advances in the engine technology, aerodynamic design and sensor systems of the J-20A, as well as the development of the two-seat variant J-20S designed to expand the aircraft's role in future air combat. The development of a domestically powered version of the J-20 marked a major milestone in the fighter's evolution. This version, powered by domestically developed engines, made its public debut at the 2021 Airshow China in Zhuhai, South China's Guangdong Province, CCTV News reported on Sunday. Wang Mingliang, a military affairs commentator, noted in the CCTV News report that the domestically developed engines provide stronger thrust, enabling the aircraft to achieve higher speeds, sustain supersonic cruise speeds and perform high-overload maneuvers. "The transition also ensures greater independence and control over the aircraft's engine system," Wang said, adding that the technological progress provides a foundation for the development of even more advanced fighter jets. The J-20A, an upgraded single-seat variant, features refinements to its aerodynamic design and sensor systems. Its modified cockpit profile is believed to improve aerodynamic performance and facilitate higher-speed flight, according to Wang. Wang pointed to two visible changes that have attracted attention among military enthusiasts. One is the raised section behind the cockpit. Compared with the earlier model, the transition between the cockpit and the aircraft's fuselage has become smoother, with a more gradual curve. "The change is likely intended to improve aerodynamic performance and increase flight speed," he said. Another change is a protruding component beneath the aircraft's nose. According to Wang, the earlier version featured six optical lenses, while the upgraded version has eight, indicating an improvement in its detection capabilities. The upgraded sensor system could give the J-20A stronger capabilities in networked and coordinated operations, including detecting and tracking stealth aircraft, Wang said. The emergence of the J-20S, a two-seat variant, represents another significant development, expanding the traditional operational role of fifth-generation fighters, the expert said, noting that the J-20S is designed to overcome some of the mission limitations of single-seat aircraft. While the pilot in the front cockpit focuses on flying and air combat, the rear-seat operator can manage unmanned aircraft formations, coordinate battlefield information, support intelligent collaboration and plan missions against targets on land and at sea. The configuration is better suited to future air combat scenarios characterized by increasing levels of intelligence, unmanned systems and networked operations. According to Wang, the J-20 is no longer simply an air-superiority fighter in the traditional sense, but can also serve as a command and coordination platform within a broader combat system. In addition to operating the aircraft's own detection and communication systems, the rear-seat operator can effectively serve as an airborne mission coordinator, helping manage information, assign targets and coordinate operations among multiple platforms, Wang said. However, advanced aircraft can realize their full potential only when integrated into an effective combat system. From initial small-scale deployment to service with multiple units and routine operations in different regions, the J-20 has increasingly become part of the PLA Air Force's broader operational framework. Its role has expanded from individual aircraft training and formation flights to participation in joint exercises, combat-oriented training and routine patrol missions. The aircraft now operates alongside other domestically developed platforms, including the KJ series of airborne early warning aircraft, YY-20 aerial refueling aircraft, J-16 multirole fighters and J-10C fighters, helping establish a more integrated air combat network. In recent years, the J-20 has expanded its operational presence, conducting routine missions in the East China Sea, South China Sea and the Taiwan Straits. Operating in complex airspace, weather and electromagnetic environments, the aircraft has continued to hone its capabilities in rapid response, all-domain operations and deterrence, CCTV News reported. The large-scale deployment and integrated use of the J-20 have helped accelerate the PLA Air Force's strategic transformation toward a force capable of conducting both offensive and defensive operations across air and space. The development of the J-20 into a family of aircraft marks an important step in China's entry into the ranks of the world's leading stealth fighter powers. Its two-seat variant is also a major innovation, representing a first of its kind globally, Chinese military affairs expert Song Zhongping told the Global Times. According to Song, the J-20 has helped place China's fifth-generation fighter capabilities at the global forefront, and further upgraded variants are expected to emerge, with increasingly advanced intelligent capabilities and stronger combat performance. "The aircraft also lays a solid foundation for the development of China's future fighter jets. For the PLA, the J-20 represents a pivotal, transitional weapon system, marking the Chinese air force's shift from following the world's leading military aviation powers to taking a leading position itself," he said.
